issues.text: Ankle swelling that starts after amlodipine is a side effect of amlodipine.
issues.problem: Stated as certain for every case. The claim record says the first question is whether the drug is the cause; Savage is dispensing data and shows an association only.
issues.source_says: C06-18-e safe wording: 'the first question is whether the drug is the cause'. Makani: oedema 10.7% on CCB vs 3.2% on control, so not every swelling is drug-caused.
issues.replacement: Ankle swelling that starts after amlodipine is often a side effect of amlodipine.

issues.text: Ankle swelling after amlodipine is a known side effect of the drug.
issues.problem: Acceptable, but for consistency the certainty should match the other versions once they are corrected.
issues.source_says: As above.
issues.replacement: Ankle swelling after amlodipine is often a side effect of the drug.

issues.text: After other blood pressure tablets the figure was about 7 in 1,000.
issues.problem: The comparator was specifically an ACE inhibitor or ARB, not blood pressure tablets in general.
issues.source_says: Savage 2020: comparator 'newly dispensed an angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitor or angiotensin II receptor blocker'; 1.4% vs 0.7% and 0.5% at 90 days.
issues.replacement: After an ACE inhibitor or ARB (another type of blood pressure tablet) the figure was about 7 in 1,000.

issues.text: In trials, adding an ACE inhibitor or ARB cut the rate of swelling by about a third
issues.problem: 'About a third' understates the result. The source is also missing from the source reply.
issues.source_says: Makani Am J Med 2011: incidence 38% lower (RR 0.62).
issues.replacement: In trials of about 9 weeks, adding an ACE inhibitor or ARB cut the rate of swelling by about 4 in 10

issues.text: Sources: Savage 2020 ... ; Makani 2011 ... ; Woodford 2020 ... ; Growdon 2025 ...
issues.problem: Leaves out Makani Am J Med 2011, the source for the ACE inhibitor/ARB figure.
issues.source_says: claims_used C06-18-e cites PMID:21295192.
issues.replacement: Sources: Savage 2020 https://doi.org/10.1001/jamainternmed.2019.7087 ; Makani 2011 (J Hypertens) https://doi.org/10.1097/HJH.0b013e3283472643 ; Makani 2011 (Am J Med) https://doi.org/10.1016/j.amjmed.2010.08.007 ; Woodford 2020 https://doi.org/10.1007/s40266-019-00730-4 ; Growdon 2025 https://doi.org/10.1001/jamanetworkopen.2025.45274

issues.text: In a UK study, 120 people taking a statin read that constipation was a 'common' side effect. On average they guessed 34 in 100
issues.problem: Subgroup written as the whole study. The 120 were split four ways (constipation or pancreatitis, word or number), so only about 30 read 'common' for constipation.
issues.source_says: Knapp 2004: 'Within each side effect condition half the patients were given the information in verbal form and half in numerical form (for constipation, "common" or 2.5%; for pancreatitis, "rare" or 0.04%)'. Mean estimate 34.2% verbal vs 8.1% numerical.
issues.replacement: In a UK study of 120 people taking a statin, those who read that constipation was a 'common' side effect guessed, on average, that 34 in 100 people would get it

issues.text: In a study in Leeds, 120 people taking a statin read that constipation was a 'common' side effect. On average they guessed that 34 in 100 people would get it.
issues.problem: Same subgroup-as-whole error as the X version.
issues.source_says: As above.
issues.replacement: In a study in Leeds of 120 people taking a statin, those who read that constipation was a 'common' side effect guessed, on average, that 34 in 100 people would get it.

issues.text: 120 statin users in Leeds; average guesses made straight after reading one statement.
issues.problem: Implies that all 120 made the guesses shown. Each bar is roughly a quarter of the sample.
issues.source_says: As above.
issues.replacement: Study of 120 statin users in Leeds, split into groups; average guesses made straight after reading one statement.

issues.text: Sources: Knapp 2004 ... ; Büchter 2014 ...
issues.problem: Leaves out Berry 2003 (C06-11-c, 'less likely to take it').
issues.source_says: claims_used C06-11-c cites PMID:12495359.

issues.text: Panel 2 caption: 'Did someone review my tablets? Nobody asked me.'
issues.problem: Invented patient quotation. It is labelled illustrative, but the patient's-eye complaint is not from the study, where patients were not interviewed.
issues.source_says: Duncan 2019: 'outside the scope of this study ... to interview patients'.
issues.replacement: Panel 2 caption: Was this review done with me, or from my notes?

issues.text: Since 2020, England has offered longer 'structured medication reviews' to some people
issues.problem: The 2020 start is background from the survey paper's introduction, not its finding. Acceptable if kept general.
issues.source_says: Agwunobi 2025 Introduction: 'SMRs were formally introduced via NHS England (NHSE) in September 2020'.
issues.replacement: Since 2020, practices in England have been able to offer longer 'structured medication reviews' to some people

issues.text: A strong pain patch still holds a substantial amount of medicine after it has been worn for its full time. Enough to seriously harm a child or a pet.
issues.problem: The residual-drug and harm-to-child evidence is for fentanyl only (Marquardt, Hilado, Finlay). 'A strong pain patch' extends it to buprenorphine without a source.
issues.source_says: Marquardt 1995 and Hilado 2020 concern fentanyl patches only.
issues.replacement: A used fentanyl pain patch still holds a substantial amount of medicine after it has been worn for its full time. Enough to seriously harm a child or a pet.

issues.text: A strong pain patch still holds a substantial amount of medicine after it has been worn for its full time. Enough to seriously harm a child or a pet.
issues.problem: Same issue as the X version.
issues.source_says: As above.
issues.replacement: A used fentanyl pain patch still holds a substantial amount of medicine after it has been worn for its full time. Enough to seriously harm a child or a pet.

issues.text: A used fentanyl or buprenorphine patch still holds a substantial amount of medicine. Enough to seriously harm a child or a pet.
issues.problem: Names buprenorphine explicitly, but no opened source covers residual buprenorphine or harm from it.
issues.source_says: The C06-08-a sources are fentanyl only.
issues.replacement: A used fentanyl patch still holds a substantial amount of medicine. Enough to seriously harm a child or a pet.

issues.text: A used strong pain patch still holds enough medicine to seriously harm a child or pet.
issues.problem: Same generalisation beyond fentanyl.
issues.source_says: As above.
issues.replacement: A used fentanyl pain patch still holds enough medicine to seriously harm a child or pet.

issues.text: A used patch still holds enough medicine to harm a child or a pet.
issues.problem: Same generalisation beyond fentanyl, on the visual.
issues.source_says: As above.
issues.replacement: A used fentanyl patch still holds enough medicine to harm a child or a pet.

issues.text: a forgotten old patch is a common route to too high a dose.
issues.problem: Incident reports cannot show how common this is.
issues.source_says: C06-08-d qualification: 'Incident reports cannot give how often this happens overall.' Lövborg: 7 of 13 too-high-dose reports.
issues.replacement: a forgotten old patch is a recognised route to too high a dose.

issues.text: Buprenorphine patches behave the same way.
issues.problem: Overstates a second-hand background statement.
issues.source_says: Thomas 2023 background: a heating pad over Butrans 'has been shown to increase systemic levels of buprenorphine in human volunteers'.
issues.replacement: Heat over a buprenorphine patch has also raised blood levels in volunteers.

issues.text: a heating pad raised fentanyl blood levels to almost 3 times higher while it was on.
issues.problem: Needs the timeframe and the small sample. Over the whole period the total dose did not differ significantly.
issues.source_says: Ashburn 2003: 10 volunteers; 'significant differences were seen during the first 4 hours, with C(max) and AUC values almost 3 times higher'; no significant difference in overall Cmax/AUC.
issues.replacement: In a small study of 10 volunteers, a heating pad raised fentanyl blood levels to almost 3 times higher during the 4 heated hours.

issues.text: MHRA https://www.gov.uk/drug-safety-update/...
issues.problem: This page was never opened (search extract only), so it should not be cited as a source. The sources for the residual-drug claim are missing.

issues.text: At 2 months, about 42 in 100 in each group were still on a medicine judged overused.
issues.problem: 'Still' implies these people were already on the medicine at baseline, which was not measured. It is a cross-sectional proportion at 2 months.
issues.source_says: OPERAM Table 5: drug overuse 42.1% control vs 41.8% intervention at 2 months, OR 0.99 (0.82 to 1.20).

issues.text: A Cochrane review of 38 trials found it uncertain whether medicines reviews reduce inappropriate prescribing
issues.problem: The Cochrane review covers 'pharmaceutical care' interventions in general, not only medicines reviews.
issues.source_says: Cole 2023: 'It is uncertain whether pharmaceutical care reduces the proportion of patients with one or more PIM ... very low-certainty evidence'.
issues.replacement: A Cochrane review of 38 trials found it uncertain whether medicines reviews and similar pharmacist-led care reduce inappropriate prescribing

issues.text: Doctors discharging older people were asked one question: will this person be harmed by their medicines in the next 8 weeks?
issues.problem: Doctors rated a likelihood of harm that needed healthcare; they did not give a yes/no to any harm. The prediction analysis covered 1,066 people, not 1,116.
issues.source_says: Parekh (prediction) 2018: doctors 'predicted the likelihood of their patient experiencing MRH requiring healthcare ... in the initial 8-week period'; 1066 analysed.
issues.replacement: Doctors discharging older people were asked how likely it was that the person would need care for harm from their medicines in the next 8 weeks.

issues.text: Doctors discharging older people were asked one question: will this person be harmed by their medicines in the next 8 weeks?
issues.problem: Same as the X version.
issues.source_says: As above.
issues.replacement: Doctors discharging older people were asked how likely it was that the person would need care for harm from their medicines in the next 8 weeks.

issues.text: The six-monthly bone injection will never be in the bag of boxes at home.
issues.problem: 'Never' is too absolute: some people are given denosumab to inject at home. The claim is a logical inference, not a finding.
issues.source_says: C06-15-c: 'The "not in the bag" point is a logical consequence of the dosing, not a study finding.'
issues.replacement: The six-monthly bone injection is usually not in the bag of boxes at home.

issues.text: Some combinations can interact, for example ginkgo, garlic or ginseng with aspirin or warfarin, with a raised bleeding risk.
issues.problem: Leaves out that these are potential interactions reported in a review, not observed harm. The LinkedIn version carries this qualification.
issues.source_says: Agbabiaka 2017: 'Potential risks of bleeding due to the use of Ginkgo biloba, garlic or ginseng with aspirin or warfarin was the most reported herb-drug interaction.'
issues.replacement: Some combinations may interact: the most often reported is a possible raised bleeding risk when ginkgo, garlic or ginseng is taken with aspirin or warfarin.

issues.text: Sources: Tam 2005 ... ; Agbabiaka 2018 ... ; Cummings 2009 ... ; Shah and Barnett 2015 ...
issues.problem: Leaves out Agbabiaka 2017, the source for the ginkgo/garlic/ginseng claim.

issues.replacement: Sources: Tam 2005 https://doi.org/10.1503/cmaj.045311 ; Agbabiaka 2018 https://doi.org/10.3399/bjgp18X699101 ; Agbabiaka 2017 https://doi.org/10.1007/s40266-017-0501-7 ; Cummings 2009 https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa0809493 ; Shah and Barnett 2015 https://doi.org/10.1002/psb.1415

issues.text: In a small US study of 40 older people on insulin, 26 had low readings over 3 days of continuous monitoring
issues.problem: Population swap. The study enrolled only people with a HIGH HbA1c (8% or more, mean 9.3%), and 37 of 40 were on insulin. In a post about low HbA1c, leaving this out suggests the study shows hidden lows in people with low HbA1c.
issues.source_says: Munshi 2011: 'Patients 69 years or older with HbA(1C) values of 8% or greater ... 37 [93%] using insulin ... Twenty-six patients (65%) experienced 1 or more episodes'.
issues.replacement: Even when HbA1c is high, lows can be missed: in a small US study of 40 older people with a high HbA1c, almost all on insulin, 26 had low readings over 3 days of continuous monitoring

issues.text: Tighter control does bring fewer blood vessel complications, so this is a balance.
issues.problem: Causal certainty drawn from a meta-analysis that mixes RCT and observational data. It also leaves out the other side of the balance, more than twice the rate of severe low sugars.
issues.source_says: Crabtree 2022: intensive control 'associated' with fewer microvascular (0.73) and macrovascular (0.84) complications; severe hypoglycaemia 2.45; no difference in mortality.
issues.replacement: Tighter control is linked with fewer blood vessel complications, but also with more than twice the rate of severe low sugars, so this is a balance.

issues.text: Sources: Hambling 2017 ... ; Strain 2018 ... ; Farrell 2017 ... ; Mattishent 2021 ... ; Munshi 2011 ...
issues.problem: Leaves out Lipska 2015 (the US national data) and Crabtree 2022 (the 15-study meta-analysis), both cited in the LinkedIn version.
issues.source_says: claims_used C06-25-a/b and C06-25-i.
issues.replacement: Sources: Hambling 2017 https://doi.org/10.1111/dme.13380 ; Lipska 2015 https://doi.org/10.1001/jamainternmed.2014.7345 ; Strain 2018 https://doi.org/10.1111/dme.13644 ; Farrell 2017 https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29138153/ ; Mattishent 2021 https://doi.org/10.3389/fendo.2021.571568 ; Munshi 2011 https://doi.org/10.1001/archinternmed.2010.539 ; Crabtree 2022 https://doi.org/10.1080/17446651.2022.2079495

issues.text: In a US hospital, a levodopa dose was missed on about 1 hospital day in 5.
issues.problem: The denominator is admission days where the home timing was known.
issues.source_says: Yu 2023: 'Of the admission days with known outpatient timing regimens ... 22% had at least one missed levodopa dose.'
issues.replacement: In a US hospital, at least one levodopa dose was missed on about 1 in 5 hospital days.

issues.text: The absolute risk is small: about 1 extra kidney injury per 158 people taking an anti-inflammatory for a year alongside both.
issues.problem: Leaves out that this figure is from the Scottish study, that injury was defined by blood tests, and that the finding is a link, not proof.
issues.source_says: Dreischulte 2015: NNH 158 for 1 year of NSAID, AKI defined as creatinine rise of 50% or more; observational.
issues.replacement: The absolute risk is small: in the Scottish study, about 1 extra kidney injury on blood tests per 158 people taking an anti-inflammatory for a year alongside both. A link, not proof of cause.

issues.text: UK studies link anti-inflammatories with these to sudden kidney injury, most with all three together, in the first month and over 75. The absolute risk is small.
issues.problem: Acceptable, but 'first month' is from the Lapi study only. Keep as is or add 'prescribed'.
issues.source_says: Lapi 2013: highest in first 30 days (RR 1.82).
issues.replacement: UK studies of prescribed anti-inflammatories link them, taken with these, to sudden kidney injury, most with all three together, in the first month and over 75. The absolute risk is small.

issues.text: A short, named list worked.
issues.problem: Presents a judgement as a finding. DQIP tested a three-part package (training, lists, payment); it did not isolate the named list, and the authors cannot say which part mattered most.
issues.source_says: Grant 2017: all components perceived active at different stages; C06-31-f: NEJM authors 'cannot identify which aspect of the intervention mattered most'.
issues.replacement: We think a short, named list is a better target than reviewing everything.

issues.text: Stomach bleeding admissions fell; kidney injury admissions showed no clear difference.
issues.problem: Leaves out that these were secondary, before-and-during comparisons (the authors say the programme 'may have improved' outcomes).
issues.source_says: Dreischulte 2016: prespecified secondary outcomes, intervention vs preintervention period.
issues.replacement: In secondary before-and-during comparisons, stomach bleeding admissions fell; kidney injury admissions showed no clear difference.

issues.text: found no difference in potentially inappropriate prescribing at 6 months.
issues.problem: House style says a non-significant result should read 'did not show a clear difference'. Here the confidence interval is tight, so this is minor.
issues.source_says: IMPPP: 'no evidence of a difference ... difference in means -0·007 [95% CI -0·21 to 0·20]'.
issues.replacement: found no evidence of a difference in potentially inappropriate prescribing at 6 months.

issues.text: About 1 in 7 older people at home find their tablets hard to swallow, and doctors often don't know.
issues.problem: Population swap. The 'doctors don't know' finding comes from a German survey of adults of all ages (difficulty was commoner in younger patients), not from older people at home.
issues.source_says: Schiele 2013: 1,051 general practice patients; 70.4% not identified by GP; age young>old.
issues.replacement: About 1 in 7 older people at home find their tablets hard to swallow. In a German GP survey of all ages, doctors had missed most cases.

issues.text: Many alter them without telling anyone.
issues.problem: Population swap and fusion of two sources. The 58.8% who altered tablets is from the all-age German survey, and 'without telling anyone' comes from a qualitative Irish interview study. Neither measured older people at home in the 1-in-7 review.
issues.source_says: Schiele 2013: 58.8% of affected all-age patients modified drugs; Mc Gillicuddy 2019 (interviews): coping without focused communication with professionals.
issues.replacement: In a German GP survey of all ages, more than half of those with difficulty had already altered their tablets themselves.

issues.text: Crushing an acid-coated tablet can stop it working.
issues.problem: 'Acid-coated' is wrong. The coating protects the tablet against stomach acid.
issues.source_says: Prescrire 2014: 'When a gastro-resistant layer is destroyed by crushing, underdosing is likely.'
issues.replacement: Crushing a tablet coated against stomach acid can stop it working properly.

issues.text: In a German GP survey of adults of all ages, doctors had not recognised 7 in 10 of those with any difficulty
issues.problem: Needs the qualification that difficulty was commoner in younger people, so readers do not apply it to older people.
issues.source_says: Schiele 2013: occurrence related to 'age (young>old)'.
issues.replacement: In a German GP survey of adults of all ages (difficulty was commoner in younger people), doctors had not recognised 7 in 10 of those with any difficulty

issues.text: Sources: Mc Gillicuddy 2016 ... ; Schiele 2013 ... ; Prescrire 2014 ... ; Saran 2022 ...
issues.problem: Leaves out Serrano Santos 2016 (nursing home figures) and Mc Gillicuddy 2019 (Irish interviews), both used in the LinkedIn version.
issues.source_says: claims_used C06-01-b, C06-01-f.
issues.replacement: Sources: Mc Gillicuddy 2016 https://doi.org/10.1007/s00228-015-1979-8 ; Schiele 2013 https://doi.org/10.1007/s00228-012-1417-0 ; Mc Gillicuddy 2019 https://doi.org/10.1016/j.sapharm.2019.01.004 ; Prescrire 2014 https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25325120/ ; Saran 2022 https://doi.org/10.3399/BJGPO.2022.0001 ; Serrano Santos 2016 https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ijpharm.2016.02.036
